items.title: 8.4 Estimating the Value of a Definite Integral

source_refs.note: Book p. 244: 8.4 Estimating the Value of a Definite Integral, introduction before 8.4.1

blocks.text: In many practical problems, however, the objective is to evaluate a definite integral of a function over a given interval. Similar to nonlinear equations, definite integrals are not always easy to evaluate analytically, and in some cases exact solutions are impossible to obtain using standard integration techniques.

For example, the integrals
\[\text{(i)}\ \int_{0}^{1} e^{-x^{2}}\,dx\]
\[\text{(ii)}\ \int_{0}^{\pi} \sin(x^{2})\,dx\]
cannot be evaluated easily by elementary methods. In such situations, numerical methods are used to estimate the value of definite integrals with reasonable accuracy.
One of the important numerical methods used for this purpose is the Trapezium Rule, which will be developed and applied in this section.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Recall how a definite integral is normally found: by the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, \(\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = F(b) - F(a)\), where \(F\) is an antiderivative of \(f\), that is \(F'(x) = f(x)\). This works only when we can write \(F\) as a formula. For \(e^{-x^{2}}\) and \(\sin(x^{2})\) mathematicians have proved that no antiderivative can be written using the usual (elementary) functions: polynomials, roots, exponentials, logarithms and trigonometric functions. So the method you learned in integration simply has nothing to substitute.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The integral itself still exists. For a positive continuous function, \(\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx\) is the area between the curve and the \(x\)-axis from \(x = a\) to \(x = b\), and every such area is a definite number. A numerical method finds that number approximately, by cutting the region into simple shapes whose areas we can compute and adding them. The same idea is used when a function is known only as a table of measured values (speed readings, rainfall, sensor data), where there is no formula to integrate at all.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Where this fits in the unit: in 8.1 to 8.3 we approximated roots (solutions of f(x) = 0) because exact formulas fail. Here the same spirit is applied to integration: accept a small, controlled error in exchange for an answer we can actually compute. The next page, 8.4.1, builds the Trapezium Rule step by step.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Some definite integrals, such as \(\int_{0}^{1} e^{-x^{2}}\,dx\) and \(\int_{0}^{\pi} \sin(x^{2})\,dx\), cannot be evaluated by elementary methods.
2. Their values still exist (an area is a number); numerical methods estimate them with reasonable accuracy.
3. The Trapezium Rule is the numerical method of this section (8.4.1).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Thinking that \"no elementary antiderivative\" means \"the integral does not exist\" or \"the answer is zero\". The integral exists whenever \(f\) is continuous on \([a, b]\); only the Fundamental Theorem route is closed, so we approximate it instead.
